title: A numerical comparison between the LANCELOT and MINOS packages for large-scale nonlinear optimization: the complete results
contribution: Data companion to Report 97/13: tabulates the dimensions of 913 CUTE test problems and the per-problem function evaluations, CPU times and coded failures of the default LANCELOT and MINOS packages.
problem_entry: Transparency: the comparison paper (97/13) gives only statistical summaries, so this report makes the complete per-problem data accessible (p. 2).
key_idea: Two table sets: problem descriptors with identities n = nfr + nfx + nb and m = nle + nne + nli + nni, from which the classes LP/QP/BC/LC/NC are derived (p. 3); then evaluations and CPU time per problem with failure codes P/T/E/F/W (pp. 27-50).
assumptions: Default options of both packages only; 12000-second CPU limit; one machine, a 333 MHz DEC Alphastation 500 (p. 27).
experiments: 913 CUTE problems. My tally of 912 parsed rows (not in the report): LANCELOT failed on 94 and MINOS on 105; where both succeeded (744), LANCELOT used fewer evaluations on 609 but MINOS less CPU on 563 (pp. 28-50).
positioning: Companion of Bongartz-Conn-Gould-Saunders-Toint Report 97/13; uses CUTE (1995) and LANCELOT (1992) (pp. 2, 51). Co-authored with Saunders, a MINOS author (p. 1; MINOS attributed to Murtagh and Saunders in S054 p. 29).
writing: Two-paragraph report, 'intended mostly for reference'; tables declared self-explanatory (pp. 2, 27).
limits_future: Defaults only, no discussion (it is in 97/13), machine-specific CPU times; no future directions (pp. 2, 27).

method_links.note: Public 913-problem CUTE set, reproducible problem descriptors, failure taxonomy including a code for optimality wrongly reported (W), complete per-problem results published separately.
Companion-report structure: discussion in 97/13, full data in 97/14.
Step 1 (fix one cost unit): the report gives evaluations and CPU time, and my tally shows the two units rank the packages in opposite directions.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The LANCELOT-MINOS comparison is co-authored by M. A. Saunders, co-author of the rival package MINOS.
Per-problem data published as a separate report so the summaries in 97/13 can be checked.

transferable: Publish every per-problem number (both cost units plus a coded failure reason) in a companion technical report cited from the main paper (pp. 2, 27).
Use a failure taxonomy with a separate code for optimality wrongly reported, to catch false successes (p. 27).
Tabulate structural descriptors with consistency identities and derive class labels from them, so labels are reproducible (p. 3).
Report two cost units (evaluations and CPU); the ranking can reverse between them (pp. 28-50).
coauthors: I. Bongartz, N. I. M. Gould, M. A. Saunders, Ph. L. Toint

quotes.text: Since we believe that complete data should be accessible to interested readers, the present companion report provides full details of the performance of each package on each problem.
It is intended mostly for reference.

title: Noise considerations in circuit optimization
contribution: Makes noise constraints (semi-infinite in time) tractable in simulation-based circuit tuning by mapping each to a time-integral equality constraint and computing all merit-function gradients in a single adjoint analysis inside JiffyTune.
problem_entry: Industrial trend: lower voltages, denser packing, faster edges and dynamic logic make noise a design criterion; noise checks are semi-infinite constraints with many signals and time windows, and no practical solution existed (p. 1).
key_idea: Replace v(x,t) >= NMH for all t by c(x) = integral of max{NMH - v, 0} dt = 0; its gradient is the integral of -dv/dx over the violation intervals, since the boundary terms vanish; gradients of the scalar Lagrangian merit function come from one adjoint analysis, whatever the number of constraints (pp. 2-4).
assumptions: Waveform continuously differentiable in x and t (p. 2); simple bounds kept satisfied so z >= 0 (p. 4); simulator and optimizer must cooperate closely (p. 4).
proof_devices: Equivalence: the integral of the positive-part violation is zero exactly when the semi-infinite constraint holds (p. 2)
Differentiation with x-dependent limits via unit steps and Dirac impulses; boundary terms cancel because the integrand is zero at the crossing times (eqs. (5)-(8), p. 3; (16)-(19), p. 5)
Adjoint excitation u(t-ts) - u(t-te) at the measurement node, weighted by the multipliers, to get the gradient of the merit function in one adjoint solve (pp. 3-4)
experiments: Dynamic AND gate tuned in 9 iterations (p. 6); delay-noise tradeoff sweep over a 50-300 mV noise margin (p. 7); branch-scan circuit (144 MOSFETs, 36 delays, 1-104 parameters, 1-459 noise functions): gradient overhead 3-18% of nominal simulation, flat in the number of noise functions (p. 7); no baseline.
positioning: Semi-infinite programming (Hettich; Hettich-Kortanek) and the Conn-Gould exact penalty for semi-infinite programming; adjoint network sensitivities (Director-Rohrer); built on JiffyTune, LANCELOT and SPECS (pp. 1-3, 6, 8).
writing: Concept demonstrated on a one-constraint example (§2) before generalizing (§3); exclamation-marked key claims about one adjoint analysis (pp. 4, 7).
limits_future: Future: static timing, wire spacing, package design, electromigration; automate generation of noise-constraint lists, which is tedious (p. 8). No convergence discussion; reader's note: the equality constraint has zero gradient at feasible points (inferred, not stated).

method_links.note: Simulator adjoints give derivatives; scalar merit-function structure exploited so one adjoint gives all gradients (Heuristic 1).
Problem from IC design trends; delivered inside the designers' tool with a schematic GUI; future work on usability.
Semi-infinite exact-penalty lineage (Conn-Gould) and LANCELOT's augmented Lagrangian reused in circuit tuning.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Differentiate the merit function, not the constraints
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Adjoint excitations weighted by the Lagrange multipliers give the gradient of the merit function in one analysis instead of one sensitivity computation per constraint.

transferable: Replace a semi-infinite constraint by the equality: integral of max{-g, 0} dt = 0, computed from the existing simulation; differentiate over the violation intervals, since the boundary terms vanish (pp. 2-3).
When the optimizer only needs the gradient of a scalar merit function, weight the adjoint excitations by the multipliers and run one adjoint analysis (p. 4).
Scaling protocol: vary #parameters and #constraints independently and plot derivative overhead as a percentage of nominal simulation (p. 7).

quotes.text: Thus a large number of noise considerations can be incorporated with a very small impact on run time.
The generation of the list of noise constraints for a large circuit can be a tedious job.

title: Two-step algorithms for nonlinear optimization with structured applications
contribution: Adds a cheap second step (in variables of known functional form) to trust-region methods, keeps global convergence by redefining the predicted reduction, shows a two-step Newton method stays q-quadratic, and applies it to slack and minimax variables in LANCELOT with CUTE and circuit results.
problem_entry: Expensive evaluations call for maximal progress per iteration; slack and minimax variables appear in a known algebraic form in LANCELOT's augmented Lagrangian, so they can be updated cheaply after each step (pp. 1, 3).
key_idea: pred = model decrease of the TR step + actual decrease of the second step (eqs. (3)-(4)); greedy (Alg. 2.2) and conservative (Alg. 2.3) variants; closed-form slack update (27) and O(m) minimax update (34)-(36) (pp. 4-5, 13-15).
assumptions: Unconstrained analysis, f in C2; bounded H_k; fraction of Cauchy decrease; for the lim-type result, uniformly continuous gradient and second step bounded by Delta or by its own decrease ((12) or (13)); extension to bounds (SBMIN) stated, not proved (pp. 2, 5, 7, 13).
proof_devices: pred inherits the Cauchy bound because the second step only adds actual decrease; |ared - pred| equals the first step's Taylor error, so Moré's argument gives liminf ||grad f|| = 0 without restricting the second step (pp. 6-7)
Acceptance-ratio monotonicity rho_hat = (t + rho)/(t + 1): the standard test's accepted steps stay accepted (Remark 3.1, p. 7)
Quadratic decrease of the second step, >= kappa ||s_hat||^2, by convexity of the slack quadratic (Prop. 5.1, pp. 13-14), then scaling so (12) or (13) holds (Alg. 3.1, p. 10)
Two-step Newton q-quadratic rate via the perturbation lemma and Lipschitz continuity of the partial gradient (Cor. 4.1, pp. 11-12)
experiments: Modified LANCELOT/SBMIN (3 versions) on 56 CUTE problems (26 non-minimax, 30 minimax): about 15% fewer iterations with named exclusions; JiffyTune dynamic-simulation circuits and static-timing minimax circuits of growing size; failure analysis of the bad minimax cases with two tested fixes (pp. 15-24).
positioning: The conservative line-search version is the Bertsekas/Luenberger spacer step; slack updates also appear in NPSOL/SNOPT; variable elimination (Golub-Pereyra) named as the alternative; analysis follows Moré's TR framework (pp. 2, 6-8, 13).
writing: Remarks that liminf convergence without a size condition may seem surprising (p. 7); states that the hoped-for Theorem 3.2 with (21) instead of (12) is unlikely to be true (p. 11); dedicated failure section §6.3.
limits_future: Unlikely to help asymptotically on small cheap problems (p. 17); on some minimax problems the second step worsens Hessian ill-conditioning (pp. 21-22); fixes tested (Table 8); general strategies left for future research (p. 23).

method_links.note: Variables of known functional form (slacks, minimax z) updated in closed form.
Class-level theorem, modified LANCELOT code and CUTE plus circuit numbers in one paper.
Two tiers reported separately (CUTE; industrial circuits) plus a size-scaling family.
Circuit evaluations taking over ten minutes justify the extra cheap step; used in JiffyTune.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: §6.3 isolates the minimax problems where two-step updating is much worse, explains the Hessian ill-conditioning mechanism and tests fixes.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Credit cheap extra decrease in the acceptance ratio
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Actual decrease of the cheap second step is added to the model's predicted decrease.

transferable: Add a cheap bonus step to a TR method by defining pred = model decrease of the TR step + actual decrease of the bonus step; for lim-type convergence bound the bonus step by Delta or by its own decrease (pp. 4-7).
Show the modified acceptance ratio increases with the bonus gain so every standard-accepted step is still accepted (p. 7).
Update slack/minimax variables of an augmented-Lagrangian subproblem in closed form after each step (pp. 13-15).
Report averages with exclusions named in both directions, then give the bad cases their own section (pp. 16, 19-24).

title: A primal-dual algorithm for minimizing a non-convex function subject to bound and linear equality constraints
contribution: A line-search primal-dual interior-point framework for non-convex objectives with bounds and linear equalities, alternating a primal-dual step and a modified barrier step on one merit function, with first-order global convergence of a subsequence and preliminary CUTE QP results.
problem_entry: Self-audit of LANCELOT: augmentation may be the wrong treatment of linear constraints, and Cauchy-point active-set prediction in SBMIN fails under degeneracy; interior-point methods are less sensitive to degeneracy; little prior non-convex primal-dual work (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Single artificial variable xi with Ax - b = xi r0; merit phi = f + rho(xi+1)^2/2 - mu<log x, e>; use the primal-dual step if it passes the descent test, else a modified barrier step; modify only N^T G N when G is not second-order sufficient (pp. 5-11).
assumptions: f in C2; iterates remain in a convex bounded subset of the positive orthant (an assumption on the iterates); A full rank; a strictly interior feasible point exists; no feasible start required (pp. 2-4).
proof_devices: Second-order sufficiency of the augmented matrix [G 0; 0 rho] w.r.t. (A r) when rho >= lambda + 2||r||^2/lambda (Lemmas 1-2, pp. 7-8)
Monotone merit function bounds the artificial variable xi (Lemma 4, (2.9)-(2.12), pp. 15-16)
Contradiction on mu bounded away from zero, with cases rho bounded / rho -> infinity (Theorem 3, p. 15; Lemmas 6-7, pp. 18, 23)
experiments: Prototype Fortran 90 QP code (MA27, pivot threshold 1e-6, G + ||G||I modification) on larger CUTE QPs vs HSL active-set VE09 (MINOS similar, not reported); reports counts of modified-barrier steps and Hessian modifications; good on convex, disappointing on non-convex (pp. 27-29).
positioning: Transplants LP primal-dual ideas (OSL, CPLEX, Shanno) to non-convex NLP; contrasts Simantiraki-Shanno (local), Forsgren-Gill (merit), Bonnans-Pola (needs interior start, convex model); linearly constrained subproblem lineage Rosen-Kreuser, Robinson, Murtagh-Saunders/MINOS (pp. 2-3).
writing: Emphasis on theory with 'preliminary' numbers; ten numbered comments on the algorithm; candid verdicts ('somewhat disappointing', 'too naive') (pp. 12-14, 29).
limits_future: Naive negative-curvature handling; KKT-matrix ill-conditioning and unsuitability of normal equations; future: trust-region variant, why primal-dual beats primal globally, role of the central path, predictor-corrector (pp. 9, 29-30).

method_links.note: Theory, prototype and CUTE numbers together; the non-convex failure drives the trust-region successor S026 (step 5).
LP primal-dual interior-point machinery transplanted into non-convex NLP, keeping LANCELOT's augmented Lagrangian for nonlinear constraints.
Linear constraints and bounds handled explicitly rather than by augmentation.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Self-audit of one's own solver starts a research line
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Named LANCELOT drawbacks (augmentation for linear constraints; Cauchy-point active-set prediction under degeneracy) motivate the method; also S089 (s01) and S124.
General NLP method tested first on non-convex QPs from CUTE, where baselines exist; repeated in S026.

transferable: Carry all linear-constraint infeasibility in one scalar xi with Ax - b = xi r0; a unit step removes it permanently (p. 5).
Compute a guaranteed-descent fallback direction from the same factorization and switch by a slope test (pp. 6-11, 14).
Modify only the reduced Hessian N^T G N so no modification is needed near a minimizer (pp. 9, 14).
Report per-problem counts of safeguard activations next to iterations and time (p. 29).
coauthors: N. I. M. Gould, Ph. L. Toint

quotes.text: In the non-convex case, the merit function is an essential ingredient of any successful algorithm and the choice of merit function was a considerable concern in the present paper.
On the other hand, its performance on the non-convex (NC) ones is somewhat disappointing.

title: A primal-dual trust-region algorithm for non-convex nonlinear programming
contribution: A primal-dual log-barrier trust-region method for non-convex objectives with linear equalities and nonlinear inequalities, globally convergent to weak second-order points even with unbounded scaling matrices, implemented as HSL VE12 and tested on CUTE QPs against the active-set VE09.
problem_entry: Redesign of the authors' own line-search method S054: assume a strictly feasible start to remove feasibility balancing, use trust regions for second-order guarantees, and separate inner and outer iterations (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Inner TR in the null space of A with the primal-dual Hessian term J^T C^-1 Z J, trust-region norm scaled by M = W + B, step rejected without evaluation if it leaves the interior (test (22)), and a safeguarded dual update by projection (pp. 6-9, 24).
assumptions: Strictly feasible x0; f, c in C2; A full rank; barrier bounded below; bounded derivatives on a region containing the iterates; dual bounds; bounded Hessian approximations; uniformly second-order-sufficient scalings; AS.9-AS.10 for second-order results (pp. 2-4, 12, 21).
proof_devices: Barrier level-set argument keeps inner iterates a fixed distance from the boundary, so radius-to-zero arguments stay inside P (Lemma 1, p. 13)
Uniform equivalence of all scaled norms within one inner minimization (Lemma 2, p. 14)
Step condition = max(Cauchy decrease, negative-curvature decrease) (19) giving first- and second-order convergence (pp. 8, 19-22)
Partition of outer iterates into finitely many 'consistently active' subsequences, and of constraints into 'eager' / 'reluctant' by z_i/c_i (pp. 26-27)
experiments: Non-convex QPs only (deliberate): VE12 with GLTR and automatic preconditioner switching, VE13 analytic-centre start, larger CUTE QPs unpreprocessed, vs VE09 with 1800 s limit; wins most small problems, non-convex as good as convex, named losses and rank-deficient failures, instances up to 100001 variables (pp. 30-34).
positioning: Direct successor of S054 (at variance with its non-convex results, p. 33); compared with Yamashita-Yabe-Tanabe, Forsgren-Gill, El-Bakry et al., Vanderbei-Shanno, Gay-Overton-Wright, Byrd-Hribar-Nocedal by merit function, indefiniteness handling and globalization (pp. 2-3).
writing: Festschrift paper for Davidon; motivations stated per design choice; assumptions defended in place (AS.4 'might at first seem strong'); explicit 'we do not pretend' on preprocessing (pp. 1-4).
limits_future: Only QPs tested; rank-deficient A unsupported; memory limits at ~1e5 variables; future: more general models agreeing to first order, general nonlinear equalities (pp. 30, 33-35).

method_links.note: Analysed algorithm shipped as HSL VE12 and tested; the redesign answers S054's numerical failure.
LP-style primal-dual interior-point ideas combined with the trio's trust-region machinery.
CUTE QPs, rival from the active-set school (VE09), iteration counts declared not comparable, named losses.
Geometry made explicit outside DFO: trust-region norm built from the model Hessian to reflect the problem's geometry; theory tolerates unbounded scalings.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Non-convex QP chosen deliberately as the prototype of linearly constrained NLP because test examples and earlier results exist; also S054.
Trial points that fail the cheap interiority test are rejected and the radius cut without evaluating the (undefined) barrier.

transferable: Reject a trial point by a cheap interiority test c(x+s) >= varsigma c(x) and shrink the radius before evaluating an undefined barrier (pp. 8-9).
Require the step to achieve the larger of a Cauchy-type and a negative-curvature decrease so one condition serves first- and second-order proofs (pp. 8-9).
Safeguard dual updates by componentwise projection onto an interval built from the iterate and mu, and prove it preserves asymptotic centrality (pp. 24-25).
Prove outer convergence on each of finitely many consistently active subsequences (p. 26).
Against an active-set code, show iterations for information only and compare CPU time with a hard limit counted as failure (p. 32).
coauthors: N. I. M. Gould, D. Orban, Ph. L. Toint

quotes.text: This was quite deliberate since we have a large number of test examples in this case, and since we already have numerical results for these examples using other QP algorithms.

We believe that this is likely because negative curvature is better handled in the trust-region subproblem than through the ad-hoc matrix modification strategy which lays at the heart of our previous linesearch algorithm.

title: A primal-dual trust-region algorithm for minimizing a non-convex function subject to general inequality and linear equality constraints
contribution: Technical-report version (Report 99/04, 16 Aug 1999) of S026 with the same algorithm, theory and tables; differences are in assumptions placement, initial-point code, hedging and abstract wording.
problem_entry: Same as S026: strictly feasible start, trust region for second-order guarantees, cleaner inner/outer split (pp. 2-3).
assumptions: Report AS.3 bounds Hessians and Jacobian over the whole feasible set (p. 4); the journal replaces it with AS.5 on a region containing the iterates (S026 p. 12). Report uses ri{P}; journal strict{P}.
proof_devices: Same as S026; report Theorems 4.4 and 4.8-4.12 correspond to journal Theorems 1-6 (pp. 13-22)
experiments: Same Tables 5.1-5.3 as S026 (pp. 26-28); initial point from HSL LA07 (p. 26) instead of VE13 in the journal.
positioning: Same as S026; the journal adds Wright (1992) and an explicit exclusion of nonlinear equalities (S026 pp. 1-2).
writing: Report says the interior-point advantages are 'now most obvious' (p. 28); the journal softens to 'clear' (S026 p. 34); abstract says 'Preliminary numerical results' (p. 2).

method_links.note: Report-then-journal pipeline: full algorithm, theory and HSL-code numbers circulated as a technical report before publication.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Report-to-journal revision localizes assumptions and softens claims
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Derivative bounds moved from the feasible set to a region containing the iterates; 'most obvious' became 'clear' (one instance).

transferable: If the proofs use derivative bounds only along the iterates, assume them on a region containing the iterates rather than on the whole feasible set (p. 4 vs S026 p. 12).
coauthors: N. I. M. Gould, D. Orban, Ph. L. Toint

quotes.text: We include these simply to show that the advantages of interior-point methods over conventional active-set approaches are now most obvious.

title: Error estimates and poisedness in multivariate polynomial interpolation
contribution: Defines a geometric, basis-independent Lambda-poisedness of interpolation sets, derives Taylor-like error bounds for the function and all derivatives (linear, quadratic, cubic), relates the condition to Lagrange-polynomial bounds, and gives a Gaussian-elimination algorithm to build or repair well-poised sets.
problem_entry: DFO trust-region theory needs Taylor-like interpolation models; existing conditions (Powell, Sauer-Xu, Waldron) are basis-tied, hard to read, or cover only function values; condition numbers are basis-dependent and can be misleading (pp. 1-2, 6).
key_idea: Y is Lambda-poised if every phi(x) - phi(0) is a combination of the phi(y_i) - phi(0) with ||lambda|| <= Lambda; equivalent to ||L^-1|| <= Lambda/Delta in the linear case and, up to constants, to bounded Lagrange polynomials; one linear system gives all derivative errors (pp. 6-10, 12-19, 24-25).
assumptions: Y in a ball centred at the origin with y0 = 0 (true in TR use, where the centre is the best point); Lipschitz gradient/Hessian/third derivatives for the linear/quadratic/cubic cases; fully determined interpolation (pp. 3-5, 19, 23).
proof_devices: Subtract the first interpolation equation from the others to cancel the function error, leaving an x-independent system L e_g = O(Delta^2) (eqs. (8)-(10), p. 8)
Equivalence of Lambda-poisedness with ||L^-1|| <= Lambda via the maximizer of ||L^-T x|| over the unit ball (Lemma 2.2, p. 9), then diagonal rescaling for radius Delta (Lemma 2.3, p. 10)
Derivative errors first, function error a posteriori (Theorem 2.4, p. 10; Theorem 3.4, p. 19)
Lower bound on the maximum of a normalized quadratic over the unit ball guarantees the pivot threshold is achievable in the repair algorithm (Lemma 3.3, p. 17; pp. 28-29)
positioning: Builds on Powell (Lagrange), Sauer-Xu (Newton) and Waldron; says the CST 1997 analysis can now be simplified and its O(Delta) gradient bound is clearly inferior; links good sets and the optimal uniform simplex to positive bases in pattern search (Audet-Dennis, Torczon, Alberto et al.) (pp. 2, 26-27, 31).
writing: Stresses intuition (calls the condition more natural; geometric reading as a 'fat' simplex); concluding remarks separate uncontrollable (smoothness) from controllable (geometry) error sources (pp. 2, 7, 31-32).
limits_future: Function-error bound does not vanish at the sample points; all-pairs system may give better constants; Newton-polynomial analysis omitted; growth-factor-dependent constants; no convergence theorem or numerics (pp. 11, 26, 29).

method_links.note: Model quality becomes an explicit basis-independent constant in every error bound, with a repair algorithm; steps 1-3 present, step 4 promised, step 5 absent.
Interpolation geometry linked to positive bases and the uniform minimal positive basis of pattern search.
Theory and algorithm without code or numbers.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Geometric definition first, then prove equivalence to the algebraic one
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Lambda-poisedness defined geometrically, shown equivalent to ||L^-1|| bounds and (up to constants) to Lagrange-polynomial bounds.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Explicitly improve one's own earlier analysis
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: States that the new gradient bound supersedes the O(Delta) bound of CST 1997, which gave only first-order convergence.

transferable: Bound all derivative errors of an interpolation model at once: Taylor-expand around the evaluation point, subtract one interpolation equation from the others, invert the x-independent matrix; get the function error from any single equation (pp. 8-10, 13-19).
Prove bounds on the unit ball, then recover Delta-dependence by diagonal rescaling (p. 10; p. 19).
Build or repair a sample set by Gaussian elimination with a pivot threshold, replacing a point by the maximizer of the pivot polynomial when needed (pp. 17, 28-29).
Check whether a condition-number quality measure depends on the basis; if so, define a basis-invariant one (p. 6).

quotes.text: To ensure the quality of the model one has to guarantee the well-poisedness of the interpolation set before seeking further accuracy by shrinking the size of the trust region (see, e.g., [3], [4]).
In practical situations only the geometry of the interpolation set is controllable.
